profile.disclosure_policy: Confirmed directly on AWS own Global Infrastructure page (aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regions_az/): AWS does not publish specific street addresses or per-building technical specifications (square footage, power capacity in MW) for its data centers, as a matter of stated security and operational policy. AWS states each Region consists of a minimum of three isolated, physically separate Availability Zones, each with independent power, cooling, and physical security, but does not break this down to individual facility addresses. This session confirmed this disclosure policy directly rather than assuming it, and applies this finding to AWS records that otherwise have no facility specific address, square footage, planned capacity, or critical_it_mw on file. This is a company wide policy finding, not a statement that no such facility exists at this location.

reading.body:
This is a building within Amazon Web Services' Northern Virginia campus, part of an infrastructure footprint spanning Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties that AWS has invested $51.9 billion into since 2011, with a further $35 billion committed through 2040. AWS does not publish per-building power capacity, square footage, or technical specifications as a stated security policy, so the critical IT load this specific facility carries cannot be independently confirmed. The building's location is mapped but remains one of hundreds of individual structures whose individual capacity contributions to the region remain opaque.

AWS states that approximately 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through Virginia data centers. Virginia ranks as one of the world's largest data center concentrations by reported volume, and AWS's announced capital commitments suggest sustained expansion of that footprint over the next 14 years. However, without published per-facility specifications, the role of individual buildings in meeting future AI scaling demand cannot be quantified.

Among Virginia's 326 mapped data center facilities, only 23 publish power capacity figures, totaling 1,375 MW. This campus building is one of the 303 facilities with no published specification, making it impossible to assess whether it represents marginal capacity, primary infrastructure, or planned future allocation. The constraint on understanding AI's grid binding problem in Virginia is not data scarcity but operator disclosure policy, which keeps facility-level capacity invisible to public analysis.
